processing: Ceylon black tea, fully oxidised. Details of the estate's current process are little documented.
harvest_season: Year-round, as is usual across Sri Lanka's hill estates.
appearance_dry: Dark brown-black leaf in the usual Ceylon grades.
appearance_liquor: Clear reddish-amber, as is typical of Kandy-side Ceylon.
taste_profile: Few notes exist on the modern tea. Teas from the Kandy hills are usually full and rounded, with moderate briskness and a malty base.

brewing.notes: Western style. A plain pot suits it, with milk if you like.

vintage_note: Not sold by vintage. Like other Ceylon estate tea it moves by grade and estate name, and should be drunk within a year or two of production. People tend to buy it for the name as much as the cup, so check the grade and date.
description:
Loolecondera is where Ceylon tea as an industry began: the first tea plantation on the island, about 35 km southeast of Kandy, near Deltota. The name is an English corruption of the Sinhala Lool Kandura, the stream full of loola fish.

James Taylor, the Scot who ran the estate, planted its first tea field and built an early factory, and it is his story that draws people here. Some of his early equipment now sits in the Ceylon Tea Museum, in the former Hanthana factory.

There is not much written about how the estate's tea tastes today. As with other Kandy-side teas, expect a rounded, moderately brisk cup with a malty base.

Drink it for the history and judge it as you would any other Ceylon: by grade and freshness. It pairs well in a side-by-side with a high-grown Dimbula, to taste what altitude does.
history:
James Joseph Mackenzie bought the land from the Crown in 1841 for coffee. It lay at 900 to 1,500 m, and its forest stayed uncleared for a decade. James Taylor arrived in Ceylon in October 1852 at 17, was sent to Loolecondera, and by 1857 was its manager.

In 1865, on the owners' instructions, he got Chinese tea seed from the Peradeniya gardens and planted it along roads and paths through the coffee, while also trying cinchona. In 1867 he cleared 19 acres and planted the first tea field with Assam hybrid seed. Coffee leaf rust then wrecked the island's coffee in the late 1860s.

A factory followed in 1872. Taylor stayed for most of his life, until his death in 1892.
